title: Cerebras and Oracle Team Up to Bring Cerebras AI Inference to OCI
content:
Oct 27 2026
Cerebras and Oracle Team Up to Bring Cerebras AI Inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Fast inference helps AI labs, enterprises, and developers build more responsive, capable AI agents and applications
LAS VEGAS, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ: CBRS) and Oracle today announced plans to make Cerebras’ fast inference available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) for AI labs, enterprises, and developers building interactive, intelligent applications. The partnership builds on Oracle’s existing infrastructure and AI inference capabilities, which include Dedicated AI Clusters in OCI Enterprise AI.
As AI applications take on more complex, multi-step work, inference speed becomes critical to the user experience. Each additional AI model call adds latency, which can slow agentic workflows that reason and act across multiple steps. Faster inference enables developers to build agents and applications that remain responsive, even as they execute more sophisticated tasks.
“People want AI that can do valuable work quickly,” said Andrew Feldman, co-founder and CEO, Cerebras. “Every step an agent makes requires inference, whether it’s reasoning, checking its work, or taking action. The faster the inference, the more work AI can do without making users wait. Bringing Cerebras fast inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives AI labs, enterprises, and developers the speed to build agents that do more, faster.”
Designed for high-speed AI inference, the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine integrates compute and memory on a single wafer-scale processor. By reducing data movement and inter-chip communication, this design supports rapid token generation for long reasoning sequences and multi-step agentic workflows.
“AI inference demands choice,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Oracle. “As agents take on more complex work, customers demand compute that matches each application’s performance needs. Bringing Cerebras’ inference to Oracle CIoud Infrastructure will add another ultrafast and deterministic option to our broad compute portfolio, helping customers build agents that respond quickly and tackle demanding tasks.”
Cerebras Inference on OCI is planned to be available in calendar year 2027, giving OCI customers another option for AI applications where speed is critical.

report.summary: Cerebras and Oracle plan to offer Cerebras’ fast AI inference on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure by 2027, targeting responsive multi-step AI agents.
report.background: The partnership arrives as AI workloads shift from training to inference, especially agentic applications that make many model calls to reason, check work, and act. Each call adds latency, so faster token generation can materially improve user experience. Cerebras is known for its Wafer-Scale Engine, which puts compute and memory on a single wafer to reduce data movement and inter-chip communication. Oracle has been expanding OCI’s AI infrastructure, including Dedicated AI Clusters in OCI Enterprise AI, and wants to offer customers compute matched to different performance needs. The announcement, made Oct. 27, 2026, is a plan rather than an immediately available product: Cerebras Inference on OCI is targeted for calendar year 2027, with no pricing or detailed availability disclosed.
key_points: Cerebras and Oracle announced plans to bring Cerebras Inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, adding an ultrafast, deterministic inference option to OCI’s compute portfolio. The companies target availability in calendar year 2027, so customers will not be able to use it immediately.

The partnership is aimed at agentic AI workflows. Because agents make multiple model calls for reasoning, verification, and actions, latency compounds. Cerebras argues faster inference keeps agents responsive even as they perform more complex, multi-step tasks.

Cerebras’ Wafer-Scale Engine integrates compute and memory on a single wafer-scale processor. By reducing data movement and inter-chip communication, the design supports rapid token generation for long reasoning sequences and multi-step agent workflows, according to the company.

Oracle already offers AI inference through Dedicated AI Clusters in OCI Enterprise AI. The Cerebras deal builds on that base and gives OCI customers another compute option for applications where speed is critical, while preserving choice across performance needs.

The release includes future-product disclaimers: timing, features, and pricing may change, and the announcement is not a contractual commitment. That makes the partnership strategically significant but still early-stage until 2027 availability is confirmed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the deal reinforces inference as the next cloud battleground. Cloud providers are diversifying beyond GPU-centric stacks and courting specialized accelerators that promise lower latency and more deterministic performance. If Cerebras Inference on OCI ships as planned, it could pressure rivals to offer similarly fast inference tiers and strengthen the case for wafer-scale and other non-GPU architectures in production AI. For developers, faster inference could shorten agent loops, reduce waiting on tool calls, and enable more interactive applications, though the 2027 timeline and unknown pricing limit near-term planning. Regular users would mainly feel the difference through snappier AI assistants and agents that complete multi-step tasks with less delay, but only after the service becomes broadly available.
report.tools: Readers can follow Cerebras Inference and its cloud/API offerings, Cerebras’ Wafer-Scale Engine documentation and SDK for developer workflows, and Oracle OCI Enterprise AI Dedicated AI Clusters to understand the existing inference stack. Also watch OCI Generative AI and Oracle Cloud infrastructure updates for 2027 availability details. For hands-on experimentation before then, developers can compare latency-sensitive agent workloads using Cerebras’ public inference services and established inference frameworks, while tracking OCI’s product announcements for pricing and access.
